parse.description: dd.xml is the Scalar Web API device descriptor: its X_ScalarWebAPI_ServiceList lists each REST service by name (system, avContent, appControl, audio, guide, ...) with an X_ScalarWebAPI_BaseURL per service. Resolve service base URLs from here rather than assuming port 80 — a service MAY live on another port. Identity fields (serial, macAddr, model, name) are NOT in dd.xml; they come from the REST call getSystemInformation on /sony/system once the client holds credentials (or immediately, on the models that answer it unauthenticated).

DIAL's SSDP response is a normal UPnP advertisement plus one extra header: LOCATION points at a UPnP device description (parsed below), and the Application-URL header carries the DIAL REST service base — on Bravia the same /DIAL tree hosts app icons, per the official getApplicationList example's http://<ip>/DIAL/icon/ URLs. The DIAL surface itself is second-screen app launching (YouTube/Netflix pairing), unauthenticated, with no power, key or volume control; it says "a DIAL-speaking Sony TV is here" but its descriptor carries no serial — REST identity (getSystemInformation) remains authoritative.

device.name: Sony Bravia IRCC-IP / REST API
device.notes: Bravia TVs (2013 and newer, including the FW-BZ professional displays) expose both surfaces on port 80: IRCC-IP at POST /sony/IRCC (SOAP action X_SendIRCC, one base64 key code per call) and the REST API as JSON-RPC-style POSTs to /sony/<service> with bodies of the form {"method": ..., "params": [...], "id": N, "version": "1.x"}. Discovery is SSDP: urn:schemas-sony-com:service:ScalarWebAPI:1 (LOCATION points at /sony/webapi/ssdp/dd.xml, which lists every REST service and its base URL) and urn:dial-multiscreen-org:service:dial:1 for DIAL second-screen discovery. Authentication is mandatory once enabled on the TV: either a pre-shared key sent as the X-Auth-PSK header, or a PIN-pairing flow (actRegister on /sony/accessControl) that ends in an auth cookie. The TV's own getRemoteControllerInfo REST call returns the model's exact IRCC key set — the static table in `commands` is Sony's published professional-display table plus widely-used community codes, and the device wins where they disagree.

openness.notes: Sony documents both surfaces for its professional displays, hence documented_api. reverse_engineered stays true because the consumer-TV behaviour this spec also covers is community-established: the PIN registration flow (actRegister, the auth cookie, its non-RFC-compliant Set-Cookie spelling), the IRCC endpoint case quirk and idle-drop quirk, and the extra consumer key codes (PowerOn, PowerOff, Exit, Rewind, Forward) come from pybravia/Home Assistant and community captures, not from Sony's pages.

upstream_docs.covers: The IRCC-IP wire format officially: POST /sony/IRCC with the SOAP envelope, the SOAPACTION and X-Auth-PSK headers, and a worked request example.

upstream_docs.covers: Sony's published key-name to base64-code table for professional displays, and the note that the same list is available on-device via getRemoteControllerInfo.
upstream_docs.title: Sony — IRCC Codes

upstream_docs.covers: Per-service, per-method request/response schemas with authentication levels (none/generic/private) and versions — getSupportedApiInfo, getApplicationList, setActiveApp, getPlayingContentInfo, getCurrentExternalInputsStatus, setPlayContent, setAudioVolume, setAudioMute, getVolumeInformation and more.

issued_to_client: auth cookie (PIN pairing only; sent as a Cookie header on every later request)
credentials.notes: No WiFi passphrase crosses any link this spec documents — it is typed into the TV. The shared secret that matters is the PSK (or the issued cookie): anything holding it has full control, so the LAN is the trust boundary. A TV that will no longer show a PIN has the client still registered — remove it via Settings > Network > Remote device settings > Deregister remote device (per the Home Assistant integration docs), then pair again.
stored_on_device: Registered remote devices (clientid/nickname list from PIN pairing)

factory_reset.effect: Clears network credentials, Google account, installed apps, the pre-shared key and every registered remote device; the TV returns to first-run setup. After a reset, IP control is off again and all pairing must be redone.

steps.action: Settings > System > About > Reset > Factory data reset (Android TV); Google TV models put Reset under Settings > System > About, older pre-Android models under Settings > Storage & reset or Customer Support. Menu spelling varies by generation — the constant is that it lives under About/System, not under Network.

For Android/Google TV models whose on-screen menu is unreachable: unplug the TV, press and hold the Power and Volume Down buttons on the TV body (not the remote), plug the TV back in while holding, and release when the reset screen or LED indication appears. Button count and exact combination vary by model — Sony's support pages distinguish one-button and three-button chassis; treat this spelling as the three-button one.
steps.notes: Reported from Sony support documentation; not exercised here.

methods.description: Two jobs, both on the TV's own screen and neither reimplementable: get the set onto the network, then enable IP control and choose its authentication. The second phase is the one every client depends on, and it is OFF until a person turns it on — which is the point of the setting.
methods.name: First-run setup, then turn on IP control

stages.description: First-run network onboarding on the TV itself: language, Google account (skippable), WiFi selection and passphrase on the on-screen keyboard. No app-driven provisioning protocol exists to reimplement.
stages.name: First-run network setup on the TV

steps.action: Power on the TV and follow the on-screen setup with the remote.
Select the WiFi network and enter the passphrase on the TV itself.

stages.description: Enable IP control and choose authentication. The client cannot do any of this remotely — that is the point of the setting.
stages.name: Turn on IP control and pick its authentication

steps.action: On the TV: Settings > Network & Internet > Remote device settings > Control remotely = On. (Older models: Settings > Network > Home Network Setup > IP Control.)

EITHER set a pre-shared key: Remote device settings > IP control > Pre-Shared Key, and hand the same string to the client, which sends it as the X-Auth-PSK header on every request. This is the flow Home Assistant recommends as the more reliable one.

OR use PIN pairing: the client POSTs actRegister to /sony/accessControl with HTTP Basic auth (empty username, password "0000") to make the TV display a PIN, then repeats the call with the shown PIN as the Basic-auth password; the TV answers 200 with an auth cookie the client sends on every later request. See bravia_common.authentication.
steps.expect: actRegister returns 200 and a Set-Cookie: auth=... header.

steps.action: Confirm the REST API is reachable and authenticated.
steps.expect: JSON result with product, model, serial, macAddr, name.

setup.notes: Two separate jobs: getting the TV on the network (done on the TV's own UI, nothing to reimplement) and enabling IP control, which is the part every client depends on and the part that is OFF until the user turns it on. "medium" rather than "high": the flow is documented by Sony and exercised daily by pybravia/Home Assistant, but this project has not run it against its own hardware. Menu spellings below are the Android TV / Google TV ones; pre-Android Bravias put the same items under Settings > Network > Home Network Setup > IP Control.

rejoin.notes: Re-running the network setup from the TV's settings joins a new router without touching anything else; the pre-shared key and registered-client list survive. A client holding an auth cookie keeps working across a network change as long as the TV's registration list is intact.

characteristics: Both IRCC-IP and the REST API on port 80; Home Assistant states support for nearly all 2013+ models.
REST service list varies by model and firmware; discover it per-device via getSupportedApiInfo on /sony/guide.

The REST surface is served by the WebApiCore system app, which community reports describe as unstable on long uptimes — a frozen API recovers with a full TV reboot or by clearing WebApiCore's data under Settings > Apps.
variants.name: Sony Bravia consumer TVs, 2013 and newer (Linux, Android TV, Google TV generations)

characteristics: The surfaces Sony itself documents: same IRCC-IP and REST API, plus 'Simple IP Control' (a fixed-format TCP byte-stream control channel) and RS-232C, per Sony's Knowledge Center. Simple IP Control is named here for completeness only; its frame format is in Sony's docs, not in this spec.
Sony's published IRCC code table (used by `commands` below) is written for this family.
variants.name: Sony Bravia Professional Displays

characteristics: IRCC-IP only: no Scalar Web API, no REST services, no getRemoteControllerInfo — key codes must come from a static table. Out of this spec's tested scope; the Home Assistant docs steer pre-2013 sets to HDMI-CEC or Broadlink instead.
variants.name: Sony Bravia TVs before 2013

entities.name: Power
entities.notes: Discrete on/off are consumer-set IRCC codes; the toggle is the one key every set carries. Prefer turn_off for a bulk send — the toggle needs the state read first, and a set with network standby off simply won't answer it.

entities.name: Power Key
entities.notes: The raw remote key, distinct from the Power switch above: it promises a keypress, not a direction. Toggle. Discrete on/off exist as press_power_on/press_power_off for consumers that ask the TV for its key list first.

entities.name: Left
entities.notes: Code disputed between Sony's pro table and community tables — see commands.press_left.

entities.name: Audio
entities.notes: Audio track/language, not a volume control.

entities.name: Input
entities.notes: Cycles inputs; the HDMI buttons below jump.

entities.name: Power Status
entities.notes: Result path: result[0].status — 'active', 'standby', ... A 'not power-on' error on other calls is this reading saying standby.

entities.name: Now Playing
entities.notes: Result path: result[0].title (with .uri/.source for detail). Blind to content inside Android apps — documented limitation, not a parsing bug.

entities.name: Volume
entities.notes: Result path: result[0][target 'speaker'].volume, 0-100 per maxVolume. authLevel none on Sony's pro reference, so this one may read even before pairing on some models.

entities.name: Application
entities.notes: No state_source: Bravia has no current-app query — Playing Content Info reports content, and inside an Android app it reports nothing. Selecting an option means POST /sony/appControl setActiveApp with {"uri": <option value>}; see the Set Active App endpoint.

documentation_review.notes: No live Bravia was probed for this spec; every command is verification "reported" — published by Sony or exercised by pybravia/Home Assistant — and nothing here carries "confirmed".

http_endpoints.description: Send one remote-key code. Case-sensitive on some models (/sony/ircc); see bravia_common.ircc.quirks. The full request template and headers are in bravia_common.ircc. The codes are in `commands` and, per model, from the Remote Controller Info call below.
http_endpoints.name: Send IRCC

http_endpoints.description: getSupportedApiInfo (v1.0, authLevel none): the device's own inventory of services, methods, versions and per-method auth levels. Call first; it is the difference between probing and knowing.
http_endpoints.name: Supported API Info

http_endpoints.description: getSystemInformation (v1.0): identity — product, model, serial, macAddr, name, generation, cid. This spec's identification source.
http_endpoints.name: System Information

http_endpoints.description: getPowerStatus (v1.0): {"result": [{"status": "active"|"standby"|...}]}. pybravia polls this on a short timeout as the TV's on/off reading.
http_endpoints.name: Power Status

http_endpoints.description: setPowerStatus (v1.0): {"status": true|false} — wake to active or drop to standby. One of the three power-on paths (bravia_common.power_on); waking only works from network standby.
http_endpoints.name: Set Power Status

http_endpoints.description: getRemoteControllerInfo (v1.0): this model's own IRCC key table — {"result": [<bundled-remote info>, [{"name": "Power", "value": "AAAA..."}, ...]]}. Authoritative over any static table (bravia_common.ircc.quirks.code_authority). Absent on pre-2013 sets.
http_endpoints.name: Remote Controller Info

http_endpoints.description: requestReboot (v1.0): reboots the TV — the supported recovery when the WebApiCore REST service freezes (device.variants).
http_endpoints.name: Request Reboot

http_endpoints.description: getVolumeInformation (v1.0, authLevel none per Sony's reference): per-target volume/mute — {"result": [[{"target": "speaker", "volume": 25, "mute": false, "minVolume": 0, "maxVolume": 100}, ...]]}.
http_endpoints.name: Volume Information

http_endpoints.description: setAudioVolume (v1.0+, authLevel generic): volume as a STRING — "25" absolute, "+1"/"-1" relative; target "speaker"|"headphone"|"". Error 40801 means out of range.
http_endpoints.name: Set Audio Volume

http_endpoints.description: setAudioMute (v1.0, authLevel generic): {"status": true|false}. There is no toggle — read Volume Information first and send the inverse, which is what pybravia's volume_mute does.
http_endpoints.name: Set Audio Mute

http_endpoints.description: getPlayingContentInfo (v1.0, authLevel private): what is on — {"result": [{"uri": "extInput:hdmi?port=2", "source": "extInput:hdmi", "title": "HDMI 2", ...}]}, or tuner programme details when the TV is the source. Knows nothing about content playing INSIDE Android apps (a documented limitation; the Home Assistant docs pair the integration with Google Cast for that).
http_endpoints.name: Playing Content Info

http_endpoints.description: getCurrentExternalInputsStatus (v1.0/v1.1, authLevel none): every input with its uri ("extInput:hdmi?port=1"), title, user label, connection and signal status. The uri is what Play Content takes — this is the input-picker's option list.
http_endpoints.name: External Inputs Status

http_endpoints.description: setPlayContent (v1.0, authLevel generic): switch to a content uri — an input ("extInput:hdmi?port=2") or a channel entry from getContentList. This is Bravia's input switching; the IRCC Hdmi1-4 keys are the key-based alternative.
http_endpoints.name: Play Content

http_endpoints.description: getApplicationList (v1.0, authLevel private): installed launchable apps — {"result": [[{"title": "YouTube", "uri": "com.sony.dtv.com.google...", "icon": "http://<ip>/DIAL/icon/..."}, ...]]}. The uri is what Set Active App takes.
http_endpoints.name: Application List

http_endpoints.description: setActiveApp (v1.0, authLevel generic): launch an app by its uri from Application List. Errors 41400/41401 mean the TV was busy — retry, don't fail the user.
http_endpoints.name: Set Active App

http_endpoints.description: terminateApps (v1.0, authLevel generic): kill all running applications.
http_endpoints.name: Terminate Apps

http_endpoints.description: setTextForm (v1.0): type a string into the TV's on-screen keyboard — Bravia's text entry; there is no Lit_-style per-character IRCC key. Error code 7 means no keyboard is on screen.
http_endpoints.name: Set Text Form

http_endpoints.description: actRegister (v1.0): PIN pairing. Full flow, including the Basic-auth password trick and the cookie, in bravia_common.authentication.
http_endpoints.name: Register Client

authentication.description: One of two credentials rides on EVERY request to /sony/*, once IP control is enabled on the TV. Which one is a per-client choice made at setup time (device.setup). A request with neither, on a TV with authentication enabled, answers 401 or 403.

pin_registration.cookie_notes: The TV's Set-Cookie spelling is not RFC-compliant (pybravia had to add a normalizer, its issue #1) — a strict cookie jar silently drops the credential and every later request fails auth. Parse the auth value out of the header string if your stack is strict.
pin_registration.description: The no-shared-secret flow. Step 1: POST actRegister with HTTP Basic auth (username "", password "0000") — the TV answers 401/403 and displays a PIN on screen. Step 2: repeat the identical call with the displayed PIN as the Basic-auth password (username still ""). On success the TV answers 200 with Set-Cookie: auth=<token>; the client sends that cookie on every later request. The pybravia request body: {"method": "actRegister", "params": [{"clientid": <client-chosen stable id, conventionally "<name>:<uuid>", "nickname": <display name>, "level": "private"}, [{"value": "yes", "function": "WOL"}]], "id": 1, "version": "1.0"} — the WOL entry asks the TV to accept wake-on-LAN from this client. A clientid already registered makes the TV refuse to show a new PIN; deregister on the TV first (device.setup.credentials).

psk.description: The string the user typed into the TV's IP control settings, sent as a plain header on every request — SOAP and REST alike. No handshake, no expiry.

bravia_common.base_url_notes: Port 80 on every documented model, but resolve per-service base URLs from dd.xml's X_ScalarWebAPI_ServiceList when available — the descriptor exists precisely because services may move ports. <ip> comes from SSDP.

dial.description: DIAL (Discovery and Launch) is the second-screen surface YouTube and Netflix use to pair a phone with the TV. Discovery is SSDP ST urn:dial-multiscreen-org:service:dial:1; the response's Application-URL header is the DIAL REST base, against which app launch/status requests are made per the DIAL 2.2.1 specification. On Bravia the same /DIAL tree hosts app icons (the official getApplicationList example returns http://<ip>/DIAL/icon/<uri>.png URLs). DIAL needs no PSK or cookie; it also exposes no power, key or volume control — it is a discovery plus app-launch channel, and this spec binds nothing to it.

ircc.description: The remote-control surface: one SOAP call per key press. POST http://<ip>/sony/IRCC with the headers below and an envelope whose only variable is the base64 IRCCCode. Success is a bare 200 with an empty (or empty-envelope) body; the TV gives no per-key feedback.

headers.X-Auth-PSK: <pre-shared key, or omit when using the auth cookie>

quirks.code_authority: Codes are model-specific in detail. The TV's own getRemoteControllerInfo REST call returns its exact name->code list and is authoritative; Sony's published table (the one in `commands`) is the professional-display set, and community tables disagree with it on some keys (Left/Right and Prev are spelled differently in the widely-copied community list). A client that can query the TV should prefer the TV's list and treat `commands` as the fallback.
quirks.endpoint_case: The path's case differs across models: /sony/IRCC on most, /sony/ircc on some — the wrong case answers 404. pybravia detects this by probing with an empty IRCCCode and swapping case on BraviaNotFound; copy that rather than shipping two configs.
quirks.idle_drop: After roughly 13 minutes of inactivity some TVs silently ignore the first IRCC command — no error, just nothing happens. pybravia works around it by sending an empty-code request as a wake-up whenever the last IRCC call is more than 10 minutes old.

power_on.description: Three documented ways to wake a Bravia, in the order pybravia tries them: a Wake-on-LAN magic packet (broadcast UDP port 9; requires the TV's Remote Start / WoL setting and the MAC from getSystemInformation), the REST call setPowerStatus {"status": true}, and the IRCC PowerOn code (AAAAAQAAAAEAAAAuAw==). All three presuppose network standby — a TV in deep standby or cut at the wall is beyond any network command, same caveat as every TV in this registry.

rest.description: Every REST service is one POST path carrying a JSON-RPC-flavoured document: {"method": "<name>", "params": [...], "id": <n>, "version": "1.x"}. params is ALWAYS an array — an empty array when the method takes nothing. A successful reply is {"result": [...], "id": <n>}; a failure is {"error": [<code>, "<message>"], "id": <n>} — and a TV in standby answers control calls with the error string "not power-on", which a client should read as "off", not "broken". Method versions and auth levels (none / generic / private) are per-method in Sony's reference; query a specific TV's actual surface with getSupportedApiInfo on /sony/guide, which is itself authLevel none.

example_request.body:
POST /sony/system HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json
X-Auth-PSK: <pre-shared key>

{"method": "getSystemInformation", "params": [], "id": 1, "version": "1.0"}
example_request.description: getSystemInformation, as it goes on the wire.

services.audio: getVolumeInformation, setAudioVolume (absolute 'N' or relative '+N'/'-N'), setAudioMute, sound settings.
services.avContent: What is playing (getPlayingContentInfo), input inventory (getCurrentExternalInputsStatus), content/channel listing (getSchemeList/getSourceList/getContentCount/getContentList), input and channel switching (setPlayContent).
services.guide: getSupportedApiInfo — the per-device API inventory; call it first.
services.system: Identity (getSystemInformation), power (getPowerStatus/setPowerStatus), getRemoteControllerInfo, getWolMode/setWolMode, requestReboot, LED indicator.
services.video/videoScreen/cec/encryption/notific: Present on various models; catalogued in Sony's reference. Out of scope for the controls this spec binds.
